**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup while you're still a student. He'd tell you to keep building the side project, and to start the company after college unless the project takes off on its own.

**Based on:** said it (high confidence). He has said this in two places, a 2014 Stanford lecture and a 2026 essay.

**Why they'd say it**
- Stanford lecture, 2014: "Do not start a startup in college." And "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s), 18:22)
- The same lecture on timing: "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s), 21:12)
- The exception he gives: "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (same moment) He means a project that takes off on its own, like Facebook.
- 2026 essay: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student. The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it." ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- On your side project specifically, he's supportive. He wants students to have free time for their own projects, because "Projects are the best source of knowledge, the best source of founding teams, and the best source of startup ideas." ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- On the unsure case: "if you're merely unsure of whether you're gonna be able to do it, the only way to find out is to try, just not now." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1438s), 23:58)

**What would change their answer:** The main condition is the one he names himself. If the project starts taking over your life, he says it may be reasonable to run with it, but then you have to choose between the company and school. In his 2026 essay he puts it bluntly: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." The 2014 remark that "You will know that it's becoming a real startup when it takes over an alarming percentage of your life" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2595s), 43:15) is the signal he gives for that.

**Caveats**
- The 2014 advice was given to Stanford students. The 2026 essay is addressed to universities and doesn't say outright what a student should do. It only says the two things don't mix.
- His advice to students comes from the founder of YC, which is where he says students go next ("We're like grad school"). He has a stake in that.
- He also admits that you can't tell in advance whether you're cut out for this, so the only test is to try it later.

**My read, not his:** His advice assumes the choice is between a full-time startup and full-time school. He doesn't address a leave of absence, a lighter course load, or working on the project part-time. If your project is taking off, those options may be worth raising with your school.

**Verdict:** Yes, he'd tell you to go, but as "for a while," not "forever." In his words: "You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go."

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He gave this advice in a talk to a Stockholm audience in April 2026. I read "need" as "does he say I should," since he uses "should," not "must."

**Why they'd say it**
- The main reason is peers: "You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 1:09)
- Serendipity: "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 3:20)
- He says the bigger effect is on you: "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 8:19)
- For Stockholm specifically, he argues returning founders help build the local hub: "you could make it the Silicon Valley of Europe. That job is still up for grabs." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 20:04)
- He also backs this with a general principle he holds: "You become like the people around you, so choose work and places by who you'll be among." ([[thinking/pg]])

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s

**Caveats, from the vault**
- He flags his own bias: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point" (@ 17:16). YC funds and profits from founders who come.
- The figure that YC startups which go home are "only about half as likely to become unicorns" (@ 18:57) is YC's internal data, given without method. He himself discounts it for selection bias.
- Altman (July 2026) agrees the Bay Area move was the best way to find co-founders, but says he has "less of an intuition for it now" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:25). So the endorsement is weaker from him.

**What would change their answer:** PG frames the case around founders' peers and the hub's critical mass. The vault doesn't cover a founder whose customers, market, or family commitments are fixed in Stockholm, so it doesn't say what he'd advise there. His own trade-off line is "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company" (@ 19:30), but he doesn't apply it to relocation.

**My read:** PG is clear that founders should go to the Valley for a while and then come back. The vault has no source saying a Stockholm founder can't build a company without moving. If you want the full case, see `startups/location/should-you-move-to-silicon-valley` and `startups/location/building-a-startup-hub-outside-the-valley` in the vault.

**Verdict:** Stop polishing the deck and stop treating follow-up meetings as the plan. Put that time into making the company something investors chase, and set a stop date for this round.

Seibel's point is that months of pitching is the mistake, not a step toward a close. A better deck can't stand in for traction.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this directly in the October 2026 episode "How Founders Win at Fundraising, Sales, and Hiring," with Dalton Caldwell ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ)).

**Why he'd say it**
- "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:03, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
- He asked investors what share of their deals they chase versus get through the front door. Answers ranged from 80/20 to 90/10 chasing. So the job is to become the company they chase. (same moment)
- When SocialCam was the number two app, the pitch deck barely mattered. (@ 9:30, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s))
- On long raises: "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a drag on the industry." (@ 6:44, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)) Caldwell adds that VCs mostly invest on traction, so meetings with a founder who isn't growing work like keeping an option open. The vault treats that as the hosts' view, not a direct quote.

**Closest analogue to your situation:** At Justin.tv, Seibel spent about eight months trying to raise. When it was clear the money wasn't coming and about two months of runway remained, the team went after profitability. He says they got more done in those two months than in the months of pitching (@ 6:44, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)).

**What that looks like for you**
1. Set a date to end the current round.
2. Ask the investors you've met whether they're chasing you or you're chasing them.
3. If they aren't chasing you, the fix is growth or revenue, not a new deck.

**What would change his answer:** If you're already growing fast and investors are coming to you, raising is cheap and the deck matters less, so keep going. The vault has no source on how to handle a round where you're growing but investors keep saying "not yet."

**Caveat:** The hosts are investors. Caldwell's fund sponsors the show, and his "investors chase most deals" point is his own read of the market. The advice to stop pitching and build is still sound, but it comes from someone on the other side of the table.

If you tell me your traction and runway, I can say which of these cases you're in.

**Verdict:** Stop the lawyer war now. Settle a no-fault, cheap, clean split: he gives back most of his stock, takes reasonable severance, signs clean paperwork, and you both walk away. Under a year in, Seibel's rule of thumb is that he keeps about 1–2% or less.

**Based on:** said it (Seibel addresses this exact situation; the percentages are rules of thumb from one 2026 episode, medium confidence on wording)

I've assumed you're the founder staying. Seibel's advice is aimed at that person.

**Why they'd say it**
- Pre-PMF, the stock is worth little, so the fight is over nothing: "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 11:36; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s)
- Vesting doesn't settle it. "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 18:39) and "Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 21:22)
- The value is ahead of you, and he's the one who gets to hedge: "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." and "you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 14:47; @ 15:21)
- Lawyers profit from the fight: "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 12:07). Also: "Any time you're spending money, be worried that someone's taking advantage." (@ 19:13)
- Don't cast a mediator as judge: "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." (@ 19:46). Caldwell's version: "the facts don't matter." (@ 9:57)
- Be the responsible party. "it is so cheap to be nice," and "if you handle this well, this is a non-mortal wound." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 17:33; @ 20:18)

**What they've done:** In the 2026 episode, the advice is framed as the YC standard, written down, with no-fault breakups as the default. "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." (@ 18:39)

**What's missing from the vault's answer**
- His equity rule assumes the company keeps going. He conditions it on "if you're pre-product market fit and the company's going to continue operating" (@ 14:47). If you're shutting down, the stock is worth nothing and the split stops mattering. The advice then is the same as the lawyer advice: stop spending money and close it out cleanly. "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." (@ 9:26)
- Don't call it dead too early. Seibel's own Justin.tv spent about eight months failing to raise, with two months of runway left, and got profitable instead ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44). Use the test he gives: do you *really know* the odds are zero?
- My inference, not his: "fewer lawyers" doesn't mean no paperwork. One lawyer drafting a short separation agreement and share-return terms is different from two sides trading letters.

**Caveats:** Several 2026 co-founder episodes are sponsored by Standard Capital, a fund Caldwell co-founded and partners in ([[profile]]). The "give back most of it" advice serves the company and its future investors, which the departing founder may reasonably see as one-sided. The percentages aren't a legal standard.

**What would change their answer**
- Misconduct. "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." (@ 21:54)
- The company having real value. Their numbers assume stock worth little.
- A company you're choosing to shut down. Then the question is how to end it cleanly, not how much equity he keeps.

I checked the key quotes and timestamps against the raw transcript for [[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]].

**Verdict:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, in the July 2026 Startup School closing conversation that Tan hosted. The vault has no statement by Tan making either claim.

**Based on:** said it (by Altman, not Tan)

- Altman, at 16:56: "I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded." ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s). The transcript is auto-captioned, so "Gary" is the caption's spelling of Garry Tan.

**Why Altman says it**

- He ties it to network effects. Right before the claim, he says the best way to find your co-founders was to move to the Bay Area, and that YC's value comes from the people you meet there. He adds that the people he started OpenAI with were people he had known for years before that. ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56 and 17:28). The vault's cofounder page makes the same point ([[finding-cofounders-and-your-people]]).
- He gives no numbers for the gap or the premium. The claim rests on his own view.

**Why the premise needs correcting**

- The vault flags this as a conflict of interest. Altman is a former YC president speaking at YC's own event, and he says so himself: "I can say this, Gary probably can't." ([[profile]]; [[finding-cofounders-and-your-people]] line 33).
- Tan's own statements in the vault are about building personal AI systems and about being "earnest" founders. His reasoning on YC's advantage is not in the vault ([[thinking/tan]]).

**What would change this answer:** a Tan-authored source with the same claim. None is in the vault now. Adding one would mean fetching more of his talks or interviews first.

**Verdict:** The vault doesn't support that premise. I found no statement where Livingston says early YC backed ruthless founders because they win. Her one use of "ruthless" in the vault describes other investors, not YC's founder selection, and she casts herself as the soft one.

**Based on:** said it (she said the opposite of the premise)

**What she actually said**
- She contrasts herself with other investors: "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s). She then describes caring how founders were feeling and counseling them through strained relationships ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 18:18).
- Her selection criteria were character, not hardness: "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s). "From the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (same timestamp).
- She judged founders on potential: "we had to judge the founders not by what they were but what they could turn into" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 16:35), and YC "had more faith in young founders than most investors did back then" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 9:46).

**Closest things to the premise**
- Boldness, not ruthlessness: "you do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1545s).
- Independence: "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 51:09; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=3069s).
- "Formidable" (someone who "gets what they want in any situation") is Paul Graham's word from September 2026, not Livingston's. The vault says it comes from a private vocabulary he shares with her ([[founders/traits/what-makes-a-founder-formidable]]). Don't attribute it to her.

**What would change this:** A source in which she says early YC preferred aggressive founders or backed the ones most likely to win. The vault has none. If you've seen this claim somewhere, send me the source and I'll check it and add it to the vault if it holds up. The claim may come from outside the vault, and I can't verify that from here.
